paper_title: Machine learning for risk stratification in the emergency department (MARS-ED): a randomized controlled trial
prediction_task: ED 31-day mortality risk stratification — RCT evaluating clinical impact

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Model showed adequate predictive accuracy but no effect on clinical decision-making or clinical outcomes. Clinical course changed for only 1 single patient of over 600 in the intervention arm. This is a 'negative example' of how NOT to implement a clinical risk score.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Reframed paper as an implementation science contribution — valuable negative example showing that even accurate models fail without workflow integration.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Insufficient detail on implementation: no information about what physicians received about the trial beforehand, how the score was integrated into workflow, what training was provided, how alert fatigue was managed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added detailed implementation strategy section with training protocol, workflow integration, and lessons learned.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Consider 7-day mortality risk instead of 31-day as avenue for better adoption. Future work should involve more user-friendly integration and risk 'zones' (e.g., infection, respiratory concern) rather than a single number.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added 7-day mortality analysis and discussed risk zone framework for future implementation.

reviewer_strengths.text: Rigorous and timely contribution to evaluation of ML-based decision support in ED. Authors have been highly responsive. The revised version reflects significant improvement.
The fact that this was implemented as part of a clinical trial where actual impact could be assessed is the main source of information. Provides valuable negative example.
